'''Peruvian Sign Language''' ({{Langx|es|Lengua de señas peruana}}, '''LSP''') is a Peruvian language created and used by the Deaf community in Peru. It has been officially recognized by Peruvian law since 2010.<ref>Ley 29535, que otorga reconocimiento oficial a la Lengua de Señas Peruanas http://docs.peru.justia.com/federales/leyes/29535-may-20-2010.pdf</ref> It is not clear how many users there are in the country; the most recent general census registered little more than 10,000,<ref name="censo2017.inei.gob.pe">''Perú: resultados definitivos.'' Vol. I. Instituto Nacional de Estadística e Informática. Lima, October 2018 http://censo2017.inei.gob.pe/</ref> but the more specific census on people with special needs found around half a million people with hearing disabilities.<ref>Encuesta Nacional sobre la Discapacidad, 2012 https://www.inei.gob.pe/media/MenuRecursivo/publicaciones_digitales/Est/Lib1171/ENEDIS%202012%20-%20COMPLETO.pdf</ref>

Variations exist in several geographically and among generations and religious groups,<ref name="Parks & Parks 2010">{{cite journal |last1=Parks |first1=Elizabeth |last2=Parks |first2=Jason |title=A Sociolinguistic Profile of the Peruvian Deaf Community |journal=Sign Language Studies |date=2010 |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=409–441 |doi=10.1353/sls.0.0054 |jstor=26190600 |s2cid=144702529 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Clark |first1=Brenda |title=Sign Language Varieties in Lima, Peru |journal=Sign Language Studies |date=2017 |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=222–264 |id={{Project MUSE|648904}} |doi=10.1353/sls.2017.0003 |s2cid=152160864 }}</ref> while the variety used in [[Lima]] is the most prestigious one.  The government has tried to integrate deaf students into mainstream educational programs with no real success, resulting in low levels of education for deaf students.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Goico |first1=Sara Alida |title=The Impact of 'Inclusive' Education on the Language of Deaf Youth in Iquitos, Peru |journal=Sign Language Studies |date=2019 |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=348–374 |id={{Project MUSE|724363}} |doi=10.1353/sls.2019.0001 |s2cid=181911057 }}</ref> On the other hand, deaf social gatherings and private schools keep the Peruvian Sign Language strong.<ref name="Parks & Parks 2010"/>

==Classification==
Clark<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Clark |first1=Brenda R. |title=A Grammatical Sketch of Sivia Sign Language. |date=December 2017 |hdl=10125/62503 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> notes that Peruvian, [[Bolivian Sign Language|Bolivian]], [[Ecuadorian Sign Language|Ecuadorian]] and [[Colombian Sign Language|Colombian]] sign languages "have significant lexical similarities to each other" and "contain a certain degree of lexical influence from ASL" as well (30% in the case of LSP), at least going by the forms in national dictionaries. [[Chilean Sign Language|Chilean]] and [[Argentinian Sign Language|Argentinian]] share these traits, though to a lesser extent. Clark counts the lexical similarities to Peruvian SL as Ecuadorian (54%), Bolivian (53%), Colombian (47%), Chilean (41%), and Argentinean (33%).
